catalog_quote: 7.2.3. Consonant Length Some consonants are sounded long. This always happens in a word with no long vowels. In these words the first syllable is stressed and the next consonant is sounded long. For example, pama is sounded: pámma A second m is not put in writing because language speakers always say it that way. 7.2.4. Word Stress (see 2.4. on page 6 for more detail) In words with no long vowels the first vowel is stressed, e.g. táwura. In words with long vowels the the last long vowel is stressed, e.g. páala, muumáanya, pitáanchi, tawuráalu.

new_statements.quote: 2.4.5 STRESS has been interpreted as non-phonemic because: (a) PRIMARY STRESS can be predicted to occur on the last lengthened vowel, if any occurs, otherwise on the first non-lengthened vowel in a word. (b) SECONDARY STRESS can be predicted to occur on the vowel immediately succeeding a primarily stressed non-lengthened vowel or, in the case of a primarily stressed lengthened vowel, on a preceding lengthened vowel if any, otherwise on the first vowel of the word. Stress is quite readily affected by emphasis, mood, fast speech etc., and frequently the effect is to equalise or reverse primary and secondary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog entry for Umpila (catalog-all-2026-09-12) records no rule at all and there are no existing statements; Thompson supplies a full rule: long-vowel-attracting primary stress with initial default, plus a secondary-stress rule. The paper describes Kuuku-Ya'u (Lockhart River), which Glottolog groups under umpi1239; Thompson's 1988 AuSIL outline already held by the project in the same folder (WP-A-11 Pt.1, printed p. 6, scanned at pages/) states the identical rule for 'Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila' ('Primary Stress occurs on the last long vowel.. otherwise on the first vowel of the word'), so the rule carries over to Umpila proper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes on the last long (lengthened) vowel of the word if the word has one; in words with no long vowel it goes on the first vowel (the word-initial syllable). Stress is treated as non-phonemic because it is predictable; each phonological word carries exactly one primary stress (section 5: 'As Primary and Secondary Stress are predictable there are no emic word contrasts marked by stress alone', p. 225).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: in words without long vowels, secondary stress falls on the vowel immediately after the primarily stressed (initial) vowel, i.e. the second syllable; in words with a long vowel, secondary stress falls on a preceding long vowel if there is one, otherwise on the first vowel of the word. Word margins 'may be unstressed or marked by Secondary Stress' (section 5).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Stress is quite readily affected by emphasis, mood, fast speech etc., and frequently the effect is to equalise or reverse primary and secondary stress' (p. 217). Consonant length is predictable 'immediately following a non-lengthened vowel which is primarily stressed' (section 2.2). Bound morphemes: 'In the case of a bound morpheme it may be best to regard it as having..' (window truncated).
new_statements.identity_note: Thompson 1976 describes Kuuku-Ya'u as spoken at the Lockhart River Aboriginal Community (near Iron Range), one of the 'related dialects' there; Glottolog places Kuuku-Ya'u under umpi1239. Thompson 1988 (held by the project, same folder) extends the same stress statement explicitly to Umpila. A separate piece in the same volume (Thompson's April 1975 report) mentions Billy Clarmont's 'Umpila dialect' but says nothing about stress.

Thompson 1976'); McGarrity 2008 cites p.217 for secondary stress on ALL remaining long vowels plus a post-tonic secondary, which differs in detail from 1988 p.6 ('the preceding long vowel, if any, otherwise the first vowel') — needed only to settle the the secondary-stress rule field, not the primary coding.
